utterances.text: And is it correct that before the beginning of the war, some of the villagers left the village and went to safer places, say Rogovo?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I was minding my own business. I stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zhuniqi. As you were minding your own business and as you do not know anything about any of this, how come you know, and how can you be sure, that some persons were not members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: But I didn't see any KLA, so how can I say that there were KLA in Bellacerke? There weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, these persons, Fatos Ekrem Zhuniqi, Kasim Sejdin Zhuniqi and Eshtref Zhuniqi, are they from your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, and they are my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that they are declared KLA members?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know that they were members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And do you know -- Mr. Zhuniqi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're leaving that subject, what do you mean by do you know that they are declared KLA members?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can ask the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zhuniqi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. That was your question: Do you know that they are declared KLA members? What does that mean? Where did you get the word "declared" from?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they are mentioned in the book Feniksi i Lirise, that is the Phoenix of Freedom. And the investigator of the OTP put questions to the witness and that is what was disclosed to us in the 68 disclosure material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zhuniqi, you were given the names of three people. You said that they were your relatives or -- were your relatives. Did they live in Bellacerke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zhuniqi, is it your assertion that you know that they were not members of the KLA or that you do not know, or is it your statement that they were never members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I said I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: However, when you talked to an investigator of the OTP, you said to him that it is your assertion that they were not members of the KLA. Have you changed your position now?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I said I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zhuniqi. Finally, let me ask you about a topic that we can deal with in several ways but I'll put it to you very simply: Today, seven years later, and after everything that you knew then and that you learned subsequently, is it your assertion that aircraft of the army of Yugoslavia bombed Nogavac at the beginning of April 1999 and that the aircraft involved were MiGs?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: At that time I said this and I'm saying this again today. They were Yugoslav aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's what you said in 1999, when you gave your statement to the OSCE. That's what you said at the Milosevic trial. And that is your assertion today, right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zhuniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zhuniqi. I have very little to ask you. Mr. Visnjic, when he was talking to you mentioned a book Feniksi i Lirise. I probably pronounced that horribly. But in any event, that is a book that was discussed with you by an investigator of this Tribunal on the 29th of June. Do you remember that interview you had with Ljubomir Josefcuk [phoen] on that date?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And were you shown that book? Did you ever see that book?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote the book?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was written in your language, in the Albanian language, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. It is written in my language, but I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so it's certainly likely that it was written by an Albanian; correct? If you don't know, you can just say you don't know. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You also told Mr. Visnjic that even today you are certain that the aircraft that bombed Nogavac were Serbian aircraft. Did you actually see those aircraft? You didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I saw them myself, and when I returned from Albania I saw parts of the bombs and they had Cyrillic letters on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you didn't see any bombs at Nogavac on the day they dropped. Where did you see them after you returned from Albania?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. That day I saw only the bombing. That day I was heavily wounded. So I couldn't see that. But when I returned from Albania, as I told you, I saw the parts of the bombs and they had the Cyrillic letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where did you see parts of the bombs that had Cyrillic letters?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: In the village Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Someone showed them to you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody showed them to me but I saw them myself when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you came back from Albania, not when the actual bombing occurred, right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: At the time of the bombing, I only heard the bombing. I was heavily wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. All I'm trying to establish is the only time you saw these bombs which had Cyrillic writing on them was after you had come back from Albania?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This has been asked and answered. He said, "I couldn't see that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree it's been answered already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm satisfied if everyone believes that. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one question from me, Mr. Ackerman. The date you gave was the 29th of June. What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 2005. That's what the notes say. I don't have any personal knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, indeed. Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zhuniqi. I'm Branko Lukic, and together with my colleagues, Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic, I am Defence counsel for General Lukic before this Tribunal. I shall briefly go back to the book, the Phoenix of Freedom since you made some comments with regard to the book. Obviously it had been showed to you. Is it correct that you saw that the signatories of this book --

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We haven't got translation of the question. Could you reput the question, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic didn't finish putting his question, interpreter's note. He was interrupted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I haven't finished my question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that the saw that the signatories of this book are Agim Ceku, Hasim Thaqi, Jakup Krasniqi, Adem Demaci, Rifat Jashari, Fatmir Limaj, a total of 18 signatories? Was that shown to you, that these were the signatories of this book?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I was not interested in that, only when the investigator showed that to me. He showed me the photographs and nothing else. He didn't show me the signatures or what you're telling me now. I was not interested in those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The trouble started when the NATO bombing started in your area, right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Up until then, you went about carrying out your own business, that is to say driving buses, right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the way up to the second half of March or even the end of March, there weren't any Serb forces in your area, right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No, there weren't. Life was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, or rather, did you know at the time, the policemen in the Orahovac police station?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said about your own village, and Celine, that you did not know about any KLA presence there. Did you perhaps hear of them being present in other villages like Velika and Mala Krusa, Nogavac, Mala Hoca?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I did not hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you describe an incident which is in English paragraph 3, paragraph 2, and in the B/C/S, 3, paragraph 1, you say that you saw a squad of 16 policemen moving towards you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you made a statement to the representatives of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in that statement, you refer to the members of these forces as members of paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this Nenad that we identified today as Nenad Matic is a person you also described as a member of the paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I saw him at the massacre in Bellacerke. What he did before, I saw him in police uniform, and maybe they changed their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you remember that when you spoke to the representatives of the OSCE you described this particular person as someone who was a former employee of the wine cellar, vinarija, and that he was a member of the paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I saw him at the traffic. I saw him at the wine cellar. And I also saw him at the massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, where is the reference to the name Nenad?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, Your Honour. It's English version, I have it here, page 3, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: His name is in that paragraph, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should be. And also it's mentioned today in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that must be where it comes from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If I may assist, he also referred to this name in his testimony in the transcript of Milosevic trial, which was also tendered today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say about this group of armed people that they were wearing greenish-blue uniforms. Over these greenish-blue uniforms, did they have some kind of vests?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No, they didn't. Just camouflage uniforms, helmets, and they had white ribbons on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where those white ribbons were? Can you show on yourself?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: On their arm. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So around their upper arm, right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, here, on their arms. It's simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that they had long knives, about 30 centimetres long, right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a policeman with a knife like that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Where do you mean? On the street or in a fighting or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Either in the street or in battle? Did you ever see a policeman with that kind of knife?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: On the street, I did not see any with knives, but what I told you here was about the bridge of Belaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did your military service in the infantry, so I assume that you will be able to help now. When you say that this group of policemen walked up to you, how were they moving? In a column, in two columns? Were they running? Were they -- what position did they take? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I saw the other part of the stream. I saw the two sides of the stream. I only saw them when they came five to ten metres close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many types of uniforms did you see at that moment? What would the smallest number be?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: At that moment, the 16 policemen that I saw wore the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it is not correct that in that group of people you saw at least two types of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't say that. It was one uniform. The 16 policemen that I saw were wearing the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of uniform was it? Could you describe it for us a bit, this uniform that they all wore?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I already said that their uniform was multi-coloured uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did these policemen wear on their heads? Could you please tell me?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: They were wearing helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they have some kind of bandanas on their heads?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No, only helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that you have a problem with colours but could you tell us what the colour of those uniforms was, please?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: It's not that I don't want to describe the colour. All I can say that they were multi-coloured uniforms. There is nothing else that I can add.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You also describe one of the troops as somebody having stars on his shoulders, which denoted his rank. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Only the person who was commanding them had three or four stars.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the stars, were there any pieces of cloth, some sort of ribbons, which could have constituted his rank as well, or denoted his rank?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. I only saw three or four stars.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The person who addressed you spoke in Albanian. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: In Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the time he was addressing you, he spoke Albanian throughout; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. He only said a few words in Albanian, and then he spoke in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When he spoke Serbian, could you detect his accent? Would you say he was from Kosovo or not?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. I couldn't tell from his accent where he was from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you about some names and to see whether you know them and whether any of those people were inhabitants of your village. Mehmet Popaj?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. He's an inhabitant from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nisim Popaj?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He lives in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sahit Popaj?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Shendet Popaj?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't follow closely and I don't know whether you were asked this by Mr. Visnjic, but how about Estref Zhuniqi? I am being told that, yes, indeed, he asked you about these people so I will stop with the names here. Were you shown whether these people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, can we just for the record, I see the two names for the Popajs are not spelled on the transcript. Could we clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well we've got Shendet Popaj, I think, and also Sahit Popaj. Could you clarify the spelling of these names, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can repeat it because I can't see it anymore, and I can clarify it with the court reporter if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. What was the name you were giving to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the people's last names are Popaj and their first names are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the third and fourth ones we need the first names of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one is Mehmet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next one is Nisim, but what are the third and fourth?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's Nisim, Sahit, Shendet, with an S-h.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zhuniqi, these four persons with the name Popaj, are they all still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are all dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All dead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zhuniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I've already asked you that question. Sorry, it's my mistake. I've lost track of this. You're not normally so far down. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because my learned friend from the opposite helped us with the -- these missed names, and my question wasn't entered until the end, and it's not clear why I asked these questions at all. So if I can only finish and if the witness can answer it; if he cannot, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On you go then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us try and clarify this, Mr. Zhuniqi. In the book, Phoenix is the Freedom, were you shown in that book that these four people were listed there as the fallen fighters or the heroes of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I saw the book when the Tribunal showed it to me. As I said, I didn't know that they were KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you yet again, Mr. Zhuniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller,

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you, according to our calculation, I have three minutes left and I would like to put two or three more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Zhuniqi, did you ever see the book Feniksi i Lirise before were you shown it in June 2005 by the ICTY investigator?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Only when I was shown it by the OTP of this Tribunal, and I never saw it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you were answering the questions of the investigator about Fatos Ekrem Zhuniqi, Kasim Sejdin Zhuniqi and Eshtref Zhuniqi of not being members of the UCK, did you do so to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my knowledge. I didn't believe that they were members of the KLA, and I didn't know if they were members of the KLA or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you on this occasion, when talking to the investigator about this book, refer to your brother Avni, who you already mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. My brother Avni was KLA, and we didn't see each other for 12 months.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you volunteered this information to the investigator in 2005, again, which you had already put in your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: My last question would be: Do you know what is the distance between Krusha e Mahde, Velika Krusa and Bela Crvka, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That completes my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zhuniqi, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it, and to provide additional information. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I call the next witness, I would also wish to tender two exhibits from the bar table, which are to some extent related to this witness's testimony. It's Exhibit P2334 and P2335. This is a request for assistance that the Office of the Prosecutor sent to Serbia and Montenegro and a response that we received in regard to this, and it contains some information regarding a person that was named by this witness today, Nenad Matic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can we see the documents, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P334, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think 2334.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: 2334, sorry. And can we scroll down, please? It would be the third page, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's see now 2335. Is that 2335?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No. This is still -- the page I would like to show you is, it says at the top, 005, and that the Exhibit number is K0530291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can we see the reply now, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The reply is P2335.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there an English version?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, there is an English version, and the B/C/S original attached thereto, in the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have this in English? Can we have it in English, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this appears to be the wrong one. This is Kosovo Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't -- yes, that's not the correct page. And could we go into the English version, which is the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not have hard copies of this that we could speed this process up with?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. Court officer, I'm informed, is printing them out right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is we can't see them so we don't know whether to object or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You hopefully will see them shortly on the e-court. Well, I'm certainly none the wiser because mine is in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm informed by my case manager that we released these documents to the Defence as soon as we filed the notification for this witness. In the English version it is -- in the response it is ICTY request 1105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're only interested in the name Nenad Matic, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. At this point we are particularly interested in this request 1105 response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now on here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 2 of that, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the name that was dealt with by the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, has anyone any objection to this document being admitted to the extent of the response at 1105, paragraph 2? Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, only if this refers to Nenad Matic and not the rest of the list. The list is quite comprehensive. Therefore, we cannot state our position as regards any other name apart from Nenad Matic, and I know this has been your practice so far and I wanted to stress this yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at what I said, I've asked to you object -- if you have an objection to it being admitted to the extent of the response at 1105, paragraph 2. Now, is that not clear? Obviously not. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's obvious that only today we get the last name from this witness, or shortly before this. Now it's Nenad Matic. Before it was only Nenad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one second until I check if in fact that's accurate. I don't think it is accurate from my reading of the transcript, which is at page 6454 of the Milosevic transcript. And there you have the name at line 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And if I may assist, the name was also referred to at page 6460 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the Prosecution had the opportunity to check with this witness whether that's the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you've lost me now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They didn't try to introduce this document through the witness we had before us a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How on earth would he be able to supplement this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't know because we are confused with this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what does he know about communications from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot testify but I can tell you that this is very common first and very common last name, so it can be the same person. It does not have to be the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've got plenty of time to investigate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the problem with -- I mean, any witness could come along here and say that somebody in particular whom he describes was present and you may wish to investigate that and bring evidence to show that, in fact, the name was right but the description was inaccurate, it was somebody else. That's a common occurrence in a trial. And you've got every opportunity to refute this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall admit P2335 to the extent only at this stage of the response to request 1105, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that reminds me of one other matter which did arise when you said, Ms. Moeller, that P97, you didn't seek to admit -- have admitted because it would be tendered through another witness. It's necessary that it just is part of the record, like every other exhibit that's been referred to, so that we can put the evidence in context. We've been adopting a practice here that's less formal in the admission of documents than the Tribunal practice in other cases because we take the view that to make sense of the evidence, the documents that are referred to need to be exhibited to the extent they were referred to. And therefore, this witness, having referred to P97, we would feel free if you were unable to have it admitted through other sources later, to refer to it to the extent necessary to understand his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. And the reason why I didn't seek to tender it was that we didn't see it feasible for this witness to actually introduce a report that was done by experts, namely the metropolitan police, who investigated this site and did the exhumation and the identification procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But we take your point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is little point now in bringing in another witness at this stage. This courtroom is to be used for the delivery of the Judgement in the case of Krajisnik, which I think will be at 1.00. To be on the safe side, we I think couldn't realistically resume before 2.30, and if for some reason something happens in Krajisnik that delays the restart, then I leave it to you to alert yourselves to that, as it happens, but we will assume that we do not resume before 2.30, and thereafter, as soon as convenient after the delivery of that Judgement. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Dr. Ali Hoti. He will testify live, and his evidence relates to paragraph 72(a)(i). He also touches upon paragraph 75(c), and the evidence is also relevant for paragraphs 25 to 32, 77(a), (b) and (d).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Hoti.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, we have no LiveNote. I can't get any LiveNote. They told me to try to use the old system. I can't get that to work either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure we'll survive while they're putting it right, Mr. Ackerman. Do we really need to be dominated by technology nowadays?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we make annotations in the transcript as it goes along and -- so it is pretty helpful to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed, I agree entirely. But for the time that it will take to fix it, I think we can proceed with the witness. The witness is giving evidence live, and if you need a pen I'll send one over to you, but let's try and get by for the moment. Okay, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Hoti. Where are you from, Dr. Hoti?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I am from Krusha e Madhe village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you live in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: In Krusha e Madhe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I'm a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you practice as a doctor in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: In March 1999, I was not employed, but I practised as a doctor in my private ambulance in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we please pull up Exhibit P615, page 22, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, could I ask you to have a look at this map displayed on the monitor? It is probably very difficult to identify any names on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I suggest that we use a hard copy? I would like him to point out some locations in the municipality, but I think it's -- on my screen I couldn't read any of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you can magnify the picture on the screen. You can have it blown up at whatever part of the map you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Could we then zoom in in the Orahovac area, please, where it says "Orahovac"? Yes. Can you move it up a little bit? Little bit further? Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, can you see on this map where your village, Krusha e Madhe, is located?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could the usher assist with a pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And could you make a circle around the village.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we leave this exhibit on while I go through the testimony so he can mark some locations later on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, how big was your village in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The village of Krusha e Madhe in 1999 had 500 houses and more than 6.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Was the population in 1999 the same as in 1998? Or was it different?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: No. It was different, since in the end of 1998, after an offensive that was launched by the Serb forces on the surrounding villages, part of the population of those villages moved to Krusha e Madhe, and the number of the population in Krusha e Madhe significantly increased.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did these people who moved into Krusha e Madhe tell you which villages they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. They were coming from Zorqisht, Opterusha, Reti villages, part from Orahovac. Mainly villages that were displaced and whose population moved to Krusha e Madhe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how was the ethnic composition in Krusha e Madhe in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Before 1998, a year or two before 1998, only two Serb families lived in Krusha e Madhe. They moved to Serbia. Therefore, the population was ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would now like to take you to the day of 25 March 1999. What did you observe in your village, in Krusha e Madhe, on this day?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry, the date was 25 March 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of March 1999, early in the morning, at 4.00 a.m., the village was encircled from all sides by the Serb forces. Large military forces, Serb military forces, were moving along the main road, and they started to stop at the village, and at every 500 metres, a tank would stop. The population, out of fear, because this main road runs in the middle of the village, through the village, so the population, seeing all these forces, fled from the village and sought shelter in the hills above the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here and go a bit more into detail. You referred to Serb military forces. What kind of vehicles did you see? You already mentioned --

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: All sorts of vehicles, from tanks, APCs, Pragas, and other escort vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you also referred to a main road. Where was this main road leading to? Between which cities?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: This is the main road that links Prizren, Gjakova and Orahovac. This is the main road that passes through that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where were you observing these movements from?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: My house is about 50 or 60 metres far from this main road. I was at home that morning. Having heard the noise of the movement of these vehicles, I noticed that the vehicles had begun to stop, as I said, at each 500 metres, and the others would proceed to other parts of the village. I was very near the place where they stopped, and we began to flee the village. I moved to the inner part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How did the persons look who manned these vehicles? What kind of uniforms, if any, did they wear?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: They all had multi-coloured uniforms. They were military forces who were wearing multi-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you already mentioned that out of fear, the population fled from the village. Did you also flee from the village?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. I left the village, together with my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you flee to?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: We fled to a hill above the village and to some valleys. Since the influx was very large, we were forced to separate into two groups. Part of the population went to Krusha e Madhe, while myself and my family moved with a group that was going in the direction of Nagavc, and we went to a valley called the valley of Cili which is near Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the map again and see whether you see Nagavc on the map?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness encircled Nagavc on the map for the transcript. How many -- how many people were at the location you just referred to with you?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: People were continuously coming from other villages as well, from Krusa, from Nagavc, to that valley. So I would say there were more than 2.000 people in that valley -- 20.000, correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you talk to some of these people?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I was with them all day long, all night long. We would talk. We would observe together. I was with them at all times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So did they tell you where they were coming from, which villages?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: There were people from Hoca e Vogel, from Brestovc village, from Zorqisht, Opterusha, Reti villages. Later on people from Celine village, not all of them, but part of them, joined us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you have another look at the map and also try to mark the villages that you just referred to on this map?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, while you were in this valley, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: While we were in this valley, during the day, we could see that Krusha e Madhe was burning. You could see the smoke coming out from the houses. And later in the day, from Celine, which is also on fire, these forces, through a secondary road, went to Nagavc village, near the valley where we were, and went to Krusha e Madhe village, and from there, they could clearly see Nagavc, Krusha e Madhe and other villages, because that is the nature of the position where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And just clarify this, you said you were in a valley, so how could you observe all these things from a valley? Did you stay in the valley all day or did you move during that time?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: When they moved, they passed by in a secondary road, and they passed near there. That's when we observed them, when they went towards Krusha e Madhe. And when it was becoming dark, they wanted to show us that "we are still here" and they shot several times with various weapons, during the whole night, but there was no other major operation that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that valley?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Until the morning of the 26th. In the morning, a group which was in the same valley but a few metres away, they started to move away. They were led by an old man who had a stick in his hand and he had a piece of white cloth attached to that stick, as a sign of surrender. When they came close to us, this old man told us that somebody had told them to go towards Albania. So he didn't even stop. He was very frightened, and he moved on. The whole population, because they were frightened too, began to move away from the valley towards Nagavc and Krusha e Madhe. At the entrance of the -- of Nagavc --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I interrupt you here and take this a little bit step by step. So you're saying that when this group, led by the old man with the white flag, met your group, that you then also started moving, you and -- does that mean also the other, the 20.000 people?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what we did. We joined them. Everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in which direction did you go then?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: In the direction of the entrance of the Nagavc -- of Nagavc village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were there any Serb forces around at that point?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. At the entrance of the village, where the road separates, it goes either to Nagavc or Krusha e Madhe, the Serb forces were there and they told us that we could not go to Albania by crossing through Krusha e Madhe, because Krusha e Madhe was in flames. The houses were on fire. So we could not go that way. And we were told to go to the centre of Nagavc village at the yard, school yard. So the whole population gathered there. We stayed there for at least two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there and shorten it a little bit. Where in Nagavc did these 20.000 people stay?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: There is a yard of a school, it's an opening, it's quite big, and that's where we stayed for two hours. Some were sitting, some were standing. All of us were there. It's a school in the centre of Nagavc and the yard of the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And for how long did you stay altogether in Nagavc after that?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: For about two hours, we stayed there, and we were waiting for somebody to tell us something. So -- people were so tired then, and they began going into the houses that had not been burned. So they took shelter in those homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, how many days did you stay in Nagavc?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: We stayed until the 2nd of April, so it's about nine days. So we were in Nagavc until the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And while you were in Nagavc, were you called upon as a doctor to help injured people?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, all the time. I treated people who needed my help, wounded people, elderly, the elderly who were sick, but my equipment was very scarce. The medicines I had also were very scarce.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Jeton Duraku?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How did you come to meet him?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Jeton Duraku was a 17-year-old young man. He came that day from the direction of that hill above Krusha e Madhe, towards Nagavc. He was there together with his family. Jeton had gone in front of the others to see what was going on on the road and to tell him family whether it was safe. When Jeton arrives at Nagavc, he met a Serbian patrol who had also stopped other young people and was searching them one by one. After searching Jeton, in his wallet they saw some kind of photograph with an Albanian eagle, which is the Albanian symbol, and the letters KLA, UCK, and they told him to go in the direction of the houses and they shot him from behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what were his injuries like?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Jeton was wounded. The wound was on the lower part of his abdomen. It was open wound. It bled continuously, but Jeton was able to speak and tell us things, but minute after minute he began losing consciousness. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So was it Jeton himself who told you what had happened to him, or how did you know that this was how he was shot?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Jeton himself told me everything, because I had to speak to him for some minutes. I tried to stop the pain. He was in pain. But it was such a big wound, and we did not have an operating theatre. Without that we could not save the life of this young man. He told me where he came from, where his family was, what happened to him, and before his family came to Jeton, Jeton passed away in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, can you help us with the date of that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened on the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I ask you to clarify that? The transcript refers to 26th of April, but you said you were in Nagavc only until the 2nd, early on.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: No. Must be a mistake. 26th of March. One day after we left Krusha e Madhe. There must be a mistake there, because it was the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Hoti, do you know a man called Mehmet Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mehmet Krasniqi as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Where did you meet him first?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I knew Mehmet Krasniqi from earlier, from before that time, because he was is from Krusha e Vogel, which is very close to Krusha e Madhe. We know each other. At that time I saw him at the village of Nagavc. When Mehmet came, he was burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you remember around which date this was?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: It must have been the 27th of March, or the 28th. I'm not very sure because at that time we lost track of dates. We did not have any means of communication. There was no electricity. We did not have any radio or television and so on. But it was the 27th or the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what was the condition Mehmet was in when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: At the moment he came to Nagavc, he was burnt. This was because of an event that had happened in Krusha e Vogel. According to him, 112 men were burnt in a barn at the village. Mehmet luckily had fallen under two other men so he was alive. His hands were totally burned and his face was burned but in the parts of the face where the other bodies had not fallen on him, and I gave him first aid with whatever equipment I had and whatever medicaments I had. We stayed together for a little while, and he told me about Krusha e Vogel and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So he told you what you just said about how he came to these burn injuries?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: He said that in the village of Krusha e Vogel, all the men that were found in the village that day, so 112 men, were taken and -- were taken to a big barn and somebody had opened fire on them. Some were wounded, some died instantly. Mehmet fell. No bullet had caught him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think we discussed this already.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any other doctor tried to help Mehmet Krasniqi while he was in Nagavc?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: At the time when Mehmet left me, I think I have -- I did not see him until the moment he left for Albania, when he went to Albania. When he came back from Albania, he had met other people in the village of Nagavc, so I did not see him from the moment he left until he went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And Dr. Hoti, do you know a person named Selami Elshani?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you see him in Nagavc?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Selami Elshani is a man from the village of Reti who was displaced. He came to Krusha e Madhe. From 1998, he lived in Krusha e Madhe. And Selami, on the 27th, maybe I'm not very exact with this, maybe I'm making a mistake in dates, but you can ask him. Selami also was burned. He had even more serious burns on his body than Mehmet. So he came to Nagavc, asked for help, and they brought him to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you treated him, did he tell you what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: After I helped him, I treated him, he told me that in Krusha e Madhe, in Haxhi Cerkini's house, which is in the upper part of the village, all the men that were found in the village were gathered there, 17 of them were separated there, men from Zorqisht, Opterusha, Reti, so they were separated, and these 17 men were told to go into a room in another house, Idriz Bida's house. They then brought straw, poured petrol, and set the petrol on fire, and these people on fire. Selami, just like Mehmet, fell first and other people fell on him. And after some time, he could not remember how long it took, but it was on the same day, Selami came out of his coma, if I can call it so, he broke a window-pane, and jumped out of the window and went out, in the direction of Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're moving on from that, there are certain things that I would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If we go back to the previous one, Mehmet Krasniqi, he was injured by fire, but you also said that the 112 men had been shot at and it was as the result of that that he had other bodies on top of him protecting his body. What then happened to cause him to be burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to clarify something here. Mehmet was not wounded. He just fell down because of his fear. While the others who were wounded fell on Mehmet. So only parts that were not covered by the bodies were burned, his feet, his hands, so -- his face, while the rest of his body was covered in blood from other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question was what caused him to be burned? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Serbian forces set the place on fire. All the other ones burned -- were burned there. Only this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That wasn't part of the account and it was important for us to be clear on that. And then, if you could now deal further with the second -- or the last one, Selami Elshani. You said he came out of his coma. How did he end up in a coma in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning, when they set the place on fire, because of the smoke and the flames, he fell, and on him fell other people. So Selami survived. Other people were burned alive in that house. He's the only one. He's alive today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that also but you said that he escaped from the house when he came out of his coma. Now, that suggests he was unconscious. How did he become unconscious?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the fire started, he was burned, but not the whole of his body was burned. So mostly his face and the parts protruding out. But he was not burned to that extent that he could die from those burns. When that house was set on fire, the windows and the doors were closed, so Selami was not conscious. And these are Selami's words, what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be a little bit late but I don't know why we are taking up the time of this Court to listen to this witness tell us what someone else told him who is alive and well and can come here and tell us the story themselves. And will. Certainly Mehmet Krasniqi is going to be here to tell us what happened. And this witness seems to have detail that couldn't have come from what these witnesses told him at the time. So it's just a little distressing that we are spending time listening to this when we are going to get it straight from the horse's mouth, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's first-hand hearsay evidence and it corroborates the account that one of the survivors, Mr. Krasniqi, indeed will give later this week, and I don't see what would be the problem with listening to Dr. Hoti, who can confirm which state Mr. Krasniqi was in when he met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand certain aspects of it can be confirmed directly by this witness. But by telling us the account of how Mr. Krasniqi was injured isn't corroboration of Mr. Krasniqi's evidence, because there is only one source of that information, that's Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and that's why I actually let him only shortly follow his account of what these people told him, just put it in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand and I saw that you were anxious to confine the account as far as possible. So let's progress now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, I would like to move now on to the 1st of April. Or rather the night of the 1st of April. What happened during that night? You were still in Nagavc?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: On the night of the 1st of April, or maybe early the 2nd of April, I could say, because it was 2.00 p.m., after midnight, we were sleeping. Suddenly there was this great noise. We woke up, we wanted to see what happened. At that moment, a plane was flying very low over Nagavc. It was a great noise. It turned around on Pashtrik, which is close to the Albania border, and at the beginning, there was this fire that came and then detonations were had heard, so Nagavc was on fire. Some houses collapsed. People were distressed, terrified. They began going into their basements. They started yelling for help because people were wounded. At the house where I was staying, the roof collapsed, the window-panes broke -- were broken, and only one woman fortunately was wounded in the house where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, did you see the plane or did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: It was 2.00 in the morning, as I said. It was the noise that made us get up and go look. But we only saw this big light, the fire, that came from the airplane and we heard the noise. It was impossible to see the plane at that time. It was 2.00 in the morning and this big light that came from the plane did not allow us to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did it sound like planes you had heard before?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: It was a noise of an airplane. It was flying very low, almost over the roofs of the houses. At that time, never -- we had never seen such a -- planes flying so low before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask you between the 24th of March and the night of 1st April, did you hear NATO airplanes flying at any time?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: From the 24th, we saw the NATO airplanes every night but I would like to make a distinction here. But for those nine nights we never saw planes flying low. The planes were flying very high and the noise was not from close. So this was a different kind of noise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Hoti, were you called upon that night again to help as a doctor injured people?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. I was called to go and help. I went from house to house, wherever I could go, to the -- I went to the first house. I saw there five wounded people and one killed person who had died. I confirmed his death and he was buried there. One of them -- one of the wounded was -- had broken ribs. One of them had a slit forehead, a cut on his forehead, while the other one had broken his arm because the wall had fallen on him. There was another house where I went. There were wounded people there. In another house, there was this little girl that had her leg cut off by a grenade. I bandaged her wound. She lives today. She lives in Nagavc today but she lost her leg. There was another child --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you again. After that incident happened, what did the people in Nagavc do? Did you stay there or did you leave Nagavc at any point?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: When morning came, at dawn, people began to collect whatever clothes they had left, put them on the tractors and began to travel towards Krusa and further on towards Albania, because we feared all the time that a similar kind of bombing would happen, but also because even the houses where they were sheltered, those houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what was your condition, your personal condition, at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: In the morning, I went back to my family. I was so distressed. I began to throw up. My head was swimming. I saw these people wounded, with their parts of their bodies strewn on the soil. I got on the tractor. It was somebody else who drove the tractor. I wasn't able to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, is this actually referred to in the indictment, as an air attack?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It is referred to as shelling, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- well, we don't talk about NATO shelling, do we? But we talk about Serb shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- the reason why we didn't change the word when we amended the indictment is that at the time the strategy was that we would -- that we would try to secure as much as possible that the two indictments against Mr. Milosevic and his co-accused would be identical and not to make any changes that are not substantively wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would you do that, if you gather more information about events and the position is clearer? Why would you keep the indictments the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think the information was already there when the evidence was presented in the Milosevic case, and witnesses in their statements which represented there and here now referred to this being an airplane bombing or shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it the evidence to be that there was no actual shelling but that on the 2nd of April it was bombing?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, you said that you left Nagavc that morning. In which direction did you go?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: We went in the direction of Krusha e Madhe. We went in the centre, towards the centre of the town. We saw that Krusa was completely burned. I went by myself and I saw that it was burned. We went to Prizren and then from there to the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here again. How many people were with you on this route?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: All the people who were in the valley, with the exception of the people who were killed, about 50 of them. The rest all continued their route to Albania. As I said, with the exception of the 50, we were about 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And while you were travelling in this very long column, did anyone approach you? "You" meaning people in the column?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: In Nadovica -- Landovica village, we came across Serbian forces. There were provocations there. Some of the elderly were taken away, those traditional hats that they wear, and they played with those hats. And we heard the words there, "You have to go to Albania. Kosova is not yours. You don't have to come back. This is Serbian land." These words.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the border, who was guarding the border at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: At the border, there were policemen in blue clothes. What the Serb police used to wear all the time. While on the road, en route, we saw military forces with camouflage uniforms. At the border we were taken away all the documents that we had on us. We were forced to take off the licence plates from the vehicles and we had to hand over all our IDs and documents, everything, with the reasoning that we did not need them anymore, that we would never come back to Kosovo anymore, we would live in Albania. This is a present from NATO and Clinton. That's what you wanted. And this is what you got. And Kosova is Serbian land. This were -- these were the words that we heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And was anything else taken away from the Kosovo Albanians before they were allowed to cross the border?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I emphasised it in the statement but I'll say it again. That we crossed the border on the 3rd of April, all night before that day we stayed in a column at the border. The people who had a nicer car, a new car, had to leave their cars, take their clothes or whatever they had, and the Serbs took away their cars. So there were several cars that were taken by the Serbs in that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Hoti, I would like to take you back because I did not address one point that I wanted to discuss with you while you were still in Nagavc. While you were in Nagavc during these days, did there ever come a police or soldiers into the village?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. On the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what did they do?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: They caught me on the street. I put my hands up. Somebody with an automatic rifle, with camouflage uniform, a tall man with a moustache, dark-skinned, he took me. There were another two who were staying by the tractors with their guns ready. This one that came to me, he asked my -- for my ID. I gave him my ID. He asked for money. He took everything that I had in foreign currency. At that time I had 700 or 800 Deutschemarks, while Yugoslavian dinars, he said, "I don't need those. You keep them." After this, he asked me, "What are you doing here?" I said, "We've been displaced from Krusha e Madhe, and I live in that house there now." So he forced me to go towards that house. I have to clarify something here. There were about 300 people staying in one single house at that time. It wasn't possible to lie down because of so many people in one house. Where I was staying, we were only 80 people, but the men were staying in one room and women and children in another room.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when he took you into that house, what did he tell you to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: After he opened the door to the room where the men were, he told me to collect the money from the men. I did so. He was not satisfied with the amount. Men, because of fear, did not carry money with them. They had the money with the women and children. That's why he then went to the room where the women and children were. He kicked the door open, and I guess he was now satisfied with the amount he got there. He then ordered us to go outside in the courtyard, and he began to separate the young men on one side. In one particular moment because of the screams and cries of mothers and other women, I guess he changed his mind and told us to go back in. I was the last --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again. When you said also -- the policeman also went into the room where the women and children were --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have to object. I don't see that he was testified that it was a policeman. I don't think he has mentioned a policeman at all during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's correct. Well, no, it's not correct in relation to the border but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. But in terms of this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, these persons -- this person who robbed you of your money and who took you to the house and then also entered the room where the women and children were in, how did he -- how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: He had a camouflage uniform. He was tall, dark complexion, had a moustache. His friends had bandanas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what colour was his uniform?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The colours on their faces were red, white and blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what colour was the uniform he wore?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, because of fear, I cannot tell you exactly the colour. Now, whether it was dark blue or whether it was black, but it was camouflaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. You already mentioned that it was a very crowded situation in the houses in Nagavc. How was the situation regarding food and hygiene?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Disastrous. Adults were mainly hungry because that little food we had we had to distribute it to children and to the persons who were sick. We would eat just what we had, that little, or even stay for two or three days without any food. And not to mention hygiene conditions, no water, no electricity, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm seeing it's already after 4.30. I don't know when you wish to take the break. I have only one more aspect to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think you should finish the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Dr. Hoti, in the statement you gave in 1999, you mention the brother of your wife being missing at the time. And you didn't know at that time what happened to him. Do you know today where he is?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. On the 26th of March, 2006, that is this year, my brother-in-law, Gezim Reshiti, together with 45 other persons were identified through ADN tests, so after seven years, these persons were found, identified and reburied. In this context, I would like to mention that we have still 37 persons whom we never found, who are still unaccounted for. At least, if an ADN test could be carried out for these persons to be identified, we have no news whatsoever about these 37 persons to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Just to clarify for the sake of the transcript, it says ADN test. Do you mean a DNA test?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, DNA in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you know where the human remains of your brother-in-law were found?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The remains of 80 persons who, in 1999, after their return from Albania were buried unidentified, they were collected from a house in the exit of Krusha e Madhe, the house where the burned, the -- those still alive or those who had died were burned. So the remains were then taken for analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the place where Mehmet Krasniqi was or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is a different place. Where the wounded, the bodies, were collected and taken to a house at the exit of Krusha e Madhe, and where there they were burned, that place was visited a lot, and that place is mentioned a lot because more than 80 persons were burned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would complete my questions. I would just ask for a snapshot to be taken of the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC57, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we shall resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be General Lukic, General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Lazarevic and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a last-minute switch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have switched with the Lukic team, if that's -- with the approval of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Hoti, I want to ask you very briefly about some testimony you gave in the Milosevic case. It's at paragraph 3626. You spoke there of an offensive that the Serb forces carried out in July of 1998 against the KLA forces in Orahovac. Do you recall talking about that?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: There was an offensive in 1998. At that time, a part of the population in Orahovac and of the villages of Zorqisht and Opterusha, they moved to our village and we learned from them that there was an offensive there and that was the reason why the population was displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That was a pretty long explanation based on my question. If you'd listen to my questions and just try to answer them as best you can and as short as you can, we won't be at this quite as long. I think you said in the Milosevic case that three or 4.000 refugees came to your village from Orahovac. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Again, I would like to specify that this was the population from Orahovac and from the villages that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And your village had a population, I think, of 6.000 so adding 3.000 or 4.000 filled your village up pretty good, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, at line 17 on that page in the Milosevic transcript, Mr. Tapuskovic was questioning you and asked you about this. And he said that this offensive, quoting Mr. Tapuskovic: "Was it aimed at driving these people out of their villages or was it aimed against the KLA?" And your answer was: "No, it was against the KLA." That's also true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move ahead to March of 1999. You describe in your statement the Serb forces arriving in the area of Krusha e Madhe on 25 March at about 4.00 in the morning, 0400 hours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you talk about two tanks having stopped in front of your house.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: This is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The main road went through your village, so these were vehicles and forces that were moving along that main road, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: No. Because they would stop there and others would continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. But -- I understand that and you told us that, that they would stop occasionally but then they would move on, and this was a large --

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Those that would stop would not move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So they stayed there?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, NATO had already started their bombing campaign by the time this happened, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The NATO campaign began on the 24th, in the evening, and what I described happened the next day, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any idea why NATO didn't bomb these vehicles that were -- these tanks and APCs and everything else that were right out in the open in your village? They would have been easy targets, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: First of all, it was the first day of the NATO campaign. Secondly, NATO in most of the cases bombed during the night. And thirdly, they were mixed with the population.
